routes.description: Establish the anti-theist charge by arguing that religious claims lack adequate evidential foundations and that purported divine authority predictably corrupts moral judgment, personal autonomy, public institutions, and natural explanations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by connecting the falsity or explanatory redundancy of supernatural claims to distinctive mechanisms of harm, while showing that morality, charity, and solidarity remain available without religion and therefore do not offset or validate those mechanisms.

motionBridge.description: Show that religion adds false supernatural authority to human affairs and thereby produces pervasive harms without supplying indispensable goods.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate that naturalistic explanations better account for religious diversity, human origins, calamity, and religious texts than supernatural claims do.
Show how claims of divine authorization insulate coercion, theocracy, violence, bodily regulation, and subordination from ordinary moral correction.
Establish that innate solidarity and secular agency adequately support morality, charity, courage, and social reform without supernatural motivation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test Christianity's historical and moral credibility through disputed biblical narratives, miracle claims, inherited guilt, and divinely commanded violence.
Use civic, medical, and sectarian consequences to illustrate the practical operation of religious authority and belief.

routes.description: Defeat the sweeping indictment by presenting Christianity as a historically credible account of creation, fallenness, rescue, grace, and redemption whose adherents and institutions can produce charity, reform, civic goods, and transformed lives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if substantial religious good defeats the universal poison charge and if Christian grace supplies a coherent source of forgiveness and transformation, while objections from religious wrongdoing, secular morality, and disputed history receive burden-relevant answers.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christianity cannot be wholly poisonous because grace and Christian commitment produce material moral, personal, civic, and charitable goods.

centralBridges.description: Require the anti-theist charge to account consistently for religious benefits as well as harms rather than defining beneficial conduct as nonreligious by default.
Explain Christianity's core as undeserved rescue and forgiveness capable of sustaining repentance, sacrificial love, and personal transformation.
Defend the historical and explanatory credibility of Christian belief against claims that scripture, creation, and miracles are merely ignorant inventions.
Connect Christian conviction to durable charitable, reformist, medical, educational, and constitutional contributions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Contextualize difficult biblical violence and distinguish Christianity's central teaching from every act performed under a religious label.
Use secular oppression and inherited moral capital to challenge claims that removing religion eliminates poison or fully explains present moral norms.

sections.title: Scope of the Poison Charge and Attribution of Good and Harm
sections.rationale: Defines the motion-level burden and tests how religious motives should be attributed when believers perform charitable acts, commit harms, or participate in conduct also available to nonbelievers.

sections.title: Religious Truth, Naturalistic Explanation, and Historical Credibility
sections.rationale: Addresses whether supernatural creation, miracles, and scripture possess credible evidential support or whether evolution, religious diversity, and ordinary causation make divine agency unnecessary.

sections.title: Divine Authority, Scriptural Morality, and Human Freedom
sections.rationale: Covers the proposed mechanism by which divine commands may authorize coercion, violence, surveillance, and subordination, together with contextual defenses of biblical teaching and conduct.

sections.title: Secular Morality, Christian Grace, and Personal Transformation
sections.rationale: Tests whether morality and compassion arise independently from human solidarity or depend on common grace and inherited Christian formation, and whether forgiveness produces distinctive reform.

sections.title: Charity, Civic Institutions, and Social Consequences
sections.rationale: Compares claims about religious service, abolition, education, liberty, medicine, theocracy, sectarian conflict, and secular oppression as practical consequences bearing on the motion.
